groups.title: How browsers parse and render pages
groups.question: Users on slow phones see a blank screen for two seconds, and a screen reader user cannot find the navigation. Explain how the browser turns your HTML and CSS into a page and how your markup affects both problems.

followUps.DOM, CSSOM, and the critical rendering p: Why can a big stylesheet or a script in the head delay the first paint?
followUps.Semantic HTML and the accessibility tree: Why does a nav element help a screen reader user more than a div?

evidence.text: The browser builds a DOM from HTML and a CSSOM from CSS, then combines them before layout and paint.
CSS blocks rendering and normal scripts block HTML parsing until they are loaded and run.
Deferring scripts and keeping critical CSS small lets the page appear sooner.

notEnough: Only naming DOM and CSSOM without saying what blocks what.

misconceptions.text: Says CSS never delays the first paint.

evidence.text: Semantic elements carry built-in roles that appear in the accessibility tree.
Screen reader users use those roles to jump between regions and controls.
A plain div has no role, so assistive tools cannot tell what it is.

notEnough: Only saying semantic HTML is better practice.

groups.title: CSS layout: box model, flexbox, and grid
groups.question: You are laying out a page with a header, sidebar and main content, and inside it a row of buttons, but every box ends up wider than you set. Explain the box model and how you would choose between flexbox and grid.

followUps.The box model and box-sizing: border-box: Why does a box with width 300px and padding end up wider, and how does border-box fix it?
followUps.Flexbox for one-dimensional layouts, Gri: When would you use grid and when flexbox?

evidence.text: Every element is a box of content, padding, border and margin.
By default width covers only the content, so padding and border are added on top.
border-box makes the width include padding and border.

notEnough: Only listing the four parts of the box.

evidence.text: Flexbox lays items out in one direction, a row or a column.
Grid controls rows and columns at the same time.
A common approach is grid for page layout and flexbox inside components.

groups.title: Responsive design and JavaScript DOM manipulation
groups.question: Your page must work on phones first, and a menu button should open and close a menu without any framework. Explain how you would write the CSS and JavaScript.

followUps.Mobile-first media queries with min-widt: Why write base styles for small screens and add min-width breakpoints?
followUps.DOM manipulation: querySelector, classLi: How would you make the button toggle the menu with plain JavaScript?

evidence.text: Base styles target small screens and larger screens are added with min-width media queries.
This usually produces less CSS than overriding a desktop design for small screens.
Many users browse on phones first, so the default experience is the mobile one.

notEnough: Only saying media queries change styles at breakpoints.

evidence.text: querySelector finds the button and menu elements.
addEventListener runs code when the button is clicked.
classList.toggle adds or removes a class that CSS uses to show or hide the menu.

notEnough: Only saying you would use JavaScript to change the DOM.

groups.title: Browser DevTools and the Fetch API
groups.question: Your recipes page calls an API, and sometimes the list is empty with no error even though the server returned a 500. Explain how you would debug the request and write the fetch code correctly.

followUps.Network tab: inspecting requests, respon: What would you check in the Network tab for a failing API call?
followUps.fetch() with async/await and proper erro: Why didn't fetch throw on the 500, and how should your code handle it?

evidence.text: The Network tab lists every request the page made.
Each request shows its status code, so failures like 404 or 500 stand out.
Headers, payload and response show what was sent and what came back, along with timing.

notEnough: Only saying you would open DevTools.

evidence.text: fetch only rejects on network failures, so error status codes still resolve.
Code must check response.ok and treat bad statuses as errors.
Network errors and HTTP errors both need handling and a message for the user.

notEnough: Only saying you use try and catch.

misconceptions.text: Says fetch throws automatically for 4xx and 5xx responses.
